newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end higher in low volume session.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end higher in low volume session.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasury securities ended higher in low volume trading on Monday with many cautious market participants sticking to the sidelines ahead of key inflation data due later in the week.

A supportive technical picture and short-covering ahead of the close of futures trading sent prices decisively into the plus column in the afternoon, but market analysts said thin conditions exaggerated the move.
The benchmark 6.75 percent 30-year bond closed at 96-00/32, up 14/32 on the day to yield 7.07 percent.
The 6.125 percent two-year note ended up 2/32 at 99-22/32 to yield 6.29 percent.

"I think some people came in this morning and decided to trade from the short side," said Patrick Dimick, treasury analyst at CS First Boston. "They got no gratification all day and had to throw in the towel at the end.

Dimick said a successful weekly three- and six-month Treasury bill auction contributed to the positive late-session tone. The Treasury sold $22.2 billion in bills on Monday, with the three-month paper garnering an average yield of 5.17 percent and the six-month paper coming in at 5.30 percent.
For much of the day, the market still appeared to be mulling over the results of Friday's employment report, even as it looked ahead to inflation data later this week.

"It was kind of a day of consolidation after the big news on Friday," said Doug Schindewolf, money market economist at Smith Barney Inc. "The focus is directed toward the inflation numbers at the end of the week."
Friday's employment report showed strong gains in wages coupled with a steep drop in the jobless rate, raising the specter of wage inflation -- a key concern for policymakers at the Federal Reserve.

Many market players believe a hike in interest rates at the Federal Reserve's upcoming September 24 policy meeting is a foregone conclusion, but others are waiting for concrete signs that inflation is on the rise before banking on a rate rise.
August wholesale and consumer inflation releases, due on Thursday and Friday respectively, have taken on added importance as a result.
"There certainly is a group within the Fed that thinks higher rates are appropriate," said Schindewolf.
"They seem to need something to hang their hat on and if these inflation numbers indicate inflation is picking up, that could be their smoking gun," he added.
The main economic report of the day consisted of second-tier U.S. consumer installment credit data for the month of July, which had no tangible market impact, analysts said.
Consumer credit rose $7.7 billion in July versus a revised $6.7 billion in June. Wall Street economists had forecast July consumer credit growth of $7.2 billion in July.

A report on labor market conditions from private research firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas Inc showed that August layoffs declined by 51 percent from July, but also had little effect on Treasury price action.

The three-month Treasury bill closed down five basis points at 5.14 percent, the six-month bill ended off four basis points at 5.31 percent and the one-year bill was down three at 5.55 percent. The Treasury's 6.5 percent five-year note ended up 6/32 at 99-11/32 to yield 6.66 percent, and the 7.0 percent 10-year note rose 10/32 to 100-26/32, yielding 6.88 percent.
